newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladeshis and wild animals flee gas fire.
newsitem.headline: Bangladeshis and wild animals flee gas fire.

text.p: Firefighters were still unable on Friday to tackle a gas field fire which has raged for five days in the country's northeast, destroying rainforest and forcing villagers and wild animals to flee.

Experts from Singapore and the United States flown in to tackle the blaze were drawing up a plan of action, but the 250 foot (76 metre) flames made it difficult for anyone to approach, oil executives said.

The fire began when a rig drilled by the U.S. oil firm Occidental Petroleum Corp hit a "trap gas" layer, sparking a blaze which ravaged two km (1.2 miles) of surrounding forest, and destroying nearby tea plantations.
"It looks like there is lot of gas in there," Ben Bearden of Occidental said. He said he did not know when his company could resume drilling at the field.

Bangladesh Energy Minister Nooruddin Khan said on Thursday it might take a month to extinguish the blaze, which has forced the evacuation of a nearby village and halted train services between Dhaka and northeast areas.
"I thought everything would perish from the unbelievable heat. Our men, women and children ran for their lives," said Shuchiang Kordor, head of the local Khasia tribe.
No-one was killed in the fire, but four Bangladeshis working at the rig were hurt.
Forest authorities have estimated losses at around two billion taka ($45 million) and are planning to demand compensation from Occidental.
The forest fire is out, but forestry workers have cut down rows of trees to try and stop the gas fire from spreading again in the dry weather conditions.
"There will be no plantations in the affected area for the next 50 years -- the fire has damaged the soil," Forest ranger Fazlur Rahman said, pointing to a swathe of burnt out trees and bald hills.
"Endangered wild animals like deer, cats, monkey and pythons have lost their habitat," he told Reuters.

The 10,000 acre (4,000 hectare) rainforest around the burning gas field has some of the region's oldest and rarest species of trees -- including a type used for making perfume -- and was declared a national park last year.
Occidental, which owns rights to explore for hydrocarbons in the entire northeastern Sylhet region, plans to spend $100 million on exploration in the area.
